claim: The androgen receptor (AR) plays a central role in the development of prostate cancer (PCa).
source: The androgen receptor (AR) plays a central role in the development of prostate cancer (PCa).
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the introduction that is supported by established scientific consensus in the field of prostate cancer research.

claim: Current approaches aimed at reducing persistent AR signaling either inhibit the production of androgens, or compete with endogenous ligands for binding to the AR C-terminal ligand-binding domain (LBD) (Helsen et al., 2014).
source: Current approaches aimed at reducing persistent AR signaling either inhibit the production of androgens, or compete with endogenous ligands for binding to the AR C-terminal ligand-binding domain (LBD) (Helsen et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Helsen et al., 2014, which provides external evidence for the statement.

claim: While these therapies are initially effective in the advanced disease setting, PCa will eventually progress to a lethal, therapy-resistant state termed castration-resistant PCa (CRPC).
source: While these therapies are initially effective in the advanced disease setting, PCa will eventually progress to a lethal, therapy-resistant state termed castration-resistant PCa (CRPC).
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about the progression of prostate cancer despite initial treatment effectiveness.

claim: In most cases of CRPC, AR continues to play a dominant role.
source: In most cases of CRPC, AR continues to play a dominant role.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field of prostate cancer research.

claim: Newer androgen synthesis inhibitors such as abiraterone and AR antagonists such as enzalutamide have been developed as second-generation therapies for the treatment of CRPC (de Bono et al., 2011; Scher et al., 2012; Beer et al., 2014).
source: Newer androgen synthesis inhibitors such as abiraterone and AR antagonists such as enzalutamide have been developed as second-generation therapies for the treatment of CRPC (de Bono et al., 2011; Scher et al., 2012; Beer et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to published research.

claim: While initially effective in the treatment of CRPC, most cases will develop resistance to these therapies (Mostaghel et al., 2014).
source: Nevertheless, while initially effective in the treatment of CRPC, most cases will develop resistance to these therapies (Mostaghel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mostaghel et al., 2014.

claim: Most of the AR transactivation function is controlled through its N-terminal activation function 1 domain (AF1), which is subdivided into the tau-1 (amino acids 100–359) and tau-5 regions (amino acids 360–528) (Claessens et al., 2008).
source: Although the AR LBD is often regarded as the major site of AR regulation, most of the AR transactivation function is controlled through its N-terminal activation function 1 domain (AF1), which is subdivided into the tau-1 (amino acids 100–359) and tau-5 regions (amino acids 360–528) (Claessens et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Claessens et al., 2008.

claim: Multiple AR variants expressed in CRPC completely lack a LBD (Guo et al., 2009).
source: Furthermore, multiple AR variants expressed in CRPC completely lack a LBD (Guo et al., 2009), illustrating the need for alternative modes of AR inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Guo et al., 2009.

claim: Targeting the AR AF-1 therapeutically has been challenging, due to its intrinsically disordered nature and lack of enzymatic activity or rigid binding clefts (Lavery and McEwan, 2008).
source: Targeting the AR AF-1 therapeutically has been challenging, due to its intrinsically disordered nature and lack of enzymatic activity or rigid binding clefts (Lavery and McEwan, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lavery and McEwan, 2008.

claim: The lack of secondary or tertiary structure of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins, such as those found in the AR AF-1 domain, could be an advantage in providing a large surface area for protein-protein interactions (Wright and Dyson, 2009).
source: However the lack of secondary or tertiary structure of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) of proteins, such as those found in the AR AF-1 domain, could be an advantage in providing a large surface area for protein-protein interactions (Wright and Dyson, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wright and Dyson, 2009.

claim: IDRs can fold upon binding to their targets, allowing them to undergo conformational changes and participate in protein complex formations (Dyson and Wright, 2005).
source: IDRs can fold upon binding to their targets, allowing them to undergo conformational changes and participate in protein complex formations (Dyson and Wright, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dyson and Wright, 2005.

claim: Interactions between IDRs and their targets tend to be more transient and of lower affinity than complex formation between structured protein regions (Latysheva et al., 2015).
source: Although these interactions tend to be more transient and of lower affinity than complex formation between structured protein regions (Latysheva et al., 2015), they have become exceedingly important for controlling the function of IDR-containing proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Latysheva et al., 2015.

claim: Bag-1 (Bcl-2-associated athanogene-1) is a multifunctional protein involved in a number of key cellular processes including proliferation, differentiation, cell cycle, transcription and apoptosis (Townsend et al., 2003a).
source: Bag-1 (Bcl-2-associated athanogene-1) is a multifunctional protein involved in a number of key cellular processes including proliferation, differentiation, cell cycle, transcription and apoptosis (Townsend et al., 2003a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Townsend et al., 2003a.

claim: The main function of Bag-1 is as a cochaperone and nucleotide exchange factor for Hsp70/Hsc70 (Alberti et al., 2003).
source: Its main function is as a cochaperone and nucleotide exchange factor for Hsp70/Hsc70 (Alberti et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alberti et al., 2003.

claim: Four Bag-1 isoforms (Bag-1L, −1M, −1 and −1S) exist in humans and are generated from the same mRNA by a leaky scanning mechanism (Takayama et al., 1998; Yang et al., 1998).
source: Four Bag-1 isoforms (Bag-1L, −1M, −1 and −1S) exist in humans and are generated from the same mRNA by a leaky scanning mechanism (Takayama et al., 1998; Yang et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Takayama et al., 1998 and Yang et al., 1998.

claim: The C-terminal (BAG) domains of Bag-1 family members are conserved and essential for interaction with Hsp70/Hsc70 (Brehmer et al., 2001; Sondermann et al., 2001).
source: Although the Bag-1 family members differ in their N-terminal domains, their C-terminal (BAG) domains are conserved and essential for interaction with Hsp70/Hsc70 (Brehmer et al., 2001; Sondermann et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Brehmer et al., 2001 and Sondermann et al., 2001.

claim: Bag-1L, the largest family member, is the only one that possesses a nuclear localization sequence and is therefore localized in the nucleus (Takayama et al., 1998).
source: Bag-1L, the largest family member, is the only one that possesses a nuclear localization sequence and is therefore localized in the nucleus (Takayama et al., 1998) where it enhances the transactivation function of several nuclear hormone receptors, including the AR (Froesch et al., 1998; Knee et al., 2001; Shatkina et al., 2003; Jehle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takayama et al., 1998.

claim: Bag-1L enhances the transactivation function of several nuclear hormone receptors, including the AR (Froesch et al., 1998; Knee et al., 2001; Shatkina et al., 2003; Jehle et al., 2014).
source: Bag-1L, the largest family member, is the only one that possesses a nuclear localization sequence and is therefore localized in the nucleus (Takayama et al., 1998) where it enhances the transactivation function of several nuclear hormone receptors, including the AR (Froesch et al., 1998; Knee et al., 2001; Shatkina et al., 2003; Jehle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Froesch et al., 1998; Knee et al., 2001; Shatkina et al., 2003; Jehle et al., 2014.

claim: Bag-1L uses a N-terminal duplicated GARRPR motif to bind to a pocket near the AR LBD, termed binding function-3 (BF-3) (Jehle et al., 2014).
source: We have recently shown that Bag-1L uses a N-terminal duplicated GARRPR motif to bind to a pocket near the AR LBD, termed binding function-3 (BF-3) (Jehle et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jehle et al., 2014.

claim: Bag-1L binds via its C-terminal BAG domain to the AR N-terminal domain (NTD) (Shatkina et al., 2003).
source: Additionally, Bag-1L binds via its C-terminal BAG domain to the AR N-terminal domain (NTD) (Shatkina et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shatkina et al., 2003.

claim: The conserved BAG domain within the C-terminus of Bag-1L selectively interacts with the intrinsically disordered, but partially folded N-terminal AR tau-5 domain.
source: Here we show that the conserved BAG domain within the C-terminus of Bag-1L selectively interacts with the intrinsically disordered, but partially folded N-terminal AR tau-5 domain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the Bag-1L BAG domain:AR tau-5 interaction by knocking out or mutating the BAG domain of Bag-1L alters the structural properties of the AR NTD and receptor folding.
source: Disrupting this interaction by knocking out or mutating the BAG domain of Bag-1L alters the structural properties of the AR NTD and receptor folding, and reduces the ability of AR to bind to chromatin and regulate transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Disrupting the Bag-1L BAG domain:AR tau-5 interaction reduces the ability of AR to bind to chromatin and regulate transcription.
source: Disrupting this interaction by knocking out or mutating the BAG domain of Bag-1L alters the structural properties of the AR NTD and receptor folding, and reduces the ability of AR to bind to chromatin and regulate transcription.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Bag-1L significantly reduced PCa growth.
source: While loss of Bag-1L significantly reduced PCa growth, re-expression of Bag-1L (but not that of the empty vector) could reverse this phenotype, confirming that LNCaP cell growth is Bag-1L dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Re-expression of Bag-1L (but not that of the empty vector) could reverse the growth reduction phenotype caused by Bag-1L loss.
source: While loss of Bag-1L significantly reduced PCa growth, re-expression of Bag-1L (but not that of the empty vector) could reverse this phenotype, confirming that LNCaP cell growth is Bag-1L dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: LNCaP cell growth is Bag-1L dependent.
source: While loss of Bag-1L significantly reduced PCa growth, re-expression of Bag-1L (but not that of the empty vector) could reverse this phenotype, confirming that LNCaP cell growth is Bag-1L dependent.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that Bag-1L loss reduces growth and re-expression restores it.

claim: AR binding increased in response to DHT in the control cells.
source: As previously reported (Wang et al., 2009), AR binding increased in response to DHT in the control cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by both a citation to Wang et al., 2009 and experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Increase in AR binding was modest in the Bag-1L KO cells, and peaks were overall weaker than those observed in the control cells.
source: In comparison, increase in AR binding was modest in the Bag-1L KO cells, and peaks were overall weaker than those observed in the control cells (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Bag-1L is necessary for effective AR binding to chromatin.
source: This implies that Bag-1L is necessary for effective AR binding to chromatin.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing reduced AR binding in Bag-1L KO cells.

claim: Bag-1L re-expression, but not the re-expression of the empty vector construct, could restore the AR binding sites.
source: Concomitantly, Bag-1L re-expression, but not the re-expression of the empty vector construct, could restore the AR binding sites (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The difference in AR binding in the presence and absence of Bag-1L was independent of the duration of DHT treatment.
source: The difference in AR binding in the presence and absence of Bag-1L was independent of the duration of DHT treatment, as confirmed by directed qPCR at three AR-bound enhancers (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 599 direct AR target genes were determined in the control cells.
source: Using this approach, we determined 599 direct AR target genes in the control and 306 in the Bag-1L KO cells (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses.

claim: 306 direct AR target genes were determined in the Bag-1L KO cells.
source: Using this approach, we determined 599 direct AR target genes in the control and 306 in the Bag-1L KO cells (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from RNA-seq and ChIP-seq analyses.

claim: Most of the genes lost in response to Bag-1L KO are associated with 'androgen response' (p=3.39×10−31; q = 1.7×10−29).
source: Using the HALLMARK function from GSEA we established that most of those genes lost in response to Bag-1L KO are associated with 'androgen response' (p=3.39×10−31; q = 1.7×10−29) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), supporting our hypothesis that one of the functions of Bag-1L in PCa is to regulate AR transactivation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: One of the functions of Bag-1L in PCa is to regulate AR transactivation.
source: Using the HALLMARK function from GSEA we established that most of those genes lost in response to Bag-1L KO are associated with 'androgen response' (p=3.39×10−31; q = 1.7×10−29) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), supporting our hypothesis that one of the functions of Bag-1L in PCa is to regulate AR transactivation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that genes lost in Bag-1L KO are associated with androgen response.

claim: One of the consequences of the loss of a chaperone or cochaperone is an alteration of the folding properties of its client proteins (Balchin et al., 2016; Mayer and Bukau, 2005).
source: One of the consequences of the loss of a chaperone or cochaperone is an alteration of the folding properties of its client proteins (Balchin et al., 2016; Mayer and Bukau, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balchin et al., 2016 and Mayer and Bukau, 2005.

claim: A much attenuated (and overall lower) FRET response to DHT was observed in the Bag-1L KO compared to the control cells (i.e., mean difference of 0.24 ± 0.01 in the control versus mean difference of 0.09 ± 0.01 in the KO cells).
source: We observed a much attenuated (and overall lower) FRET response to DHT in the Bag-1L KO compared to the control cells (i.e., mean difference of 0.24 ± 0.01 in the control versus mean difference of 0.09 ± 0.01 in the KO cells).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There are significant alterations in the inter-domain interaction and folding of the AR in the absence of Bag-1L that effect the ability of the receptor to efficiently respond to DHT, bind to chromatin and regulate gene expression.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that there are significant alterations in the inter-domain interaction and folding of the AR in the absence of Bag-1L that effect the ability of the receptor to efficiently respond to DHT, bind to chromatin and regulate gene expression.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined experimental results including FRET, ChIP-seq, and RNA-seq data.

claim: Bag-1L enhances AR activity via the tau-5 domain within the AR AF-1.
source: Moreover, Bag-1L enhances AR activity via the tau-5 domain within the AR AF-1 (Shatkina et al., 2003) (Figure 2B), a region known for its hormone-independent receptor activity (Jenster et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shatkina et al., 2003 and experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The tau-5 domain is a region known for its hormone-independent receptor activity (Jenster et al., 1995).
source: Moreover, Bag-1L enhances AR activity via the tau-5 domain within the AR AF-1 (Shatkina et al., 2003) (Figure 2B), a region known for its hormone-independent receptor activity (Jenster et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jenster et al., 1995.

claim: The interaction of AR tau-5 is with the Bag-1L BAG domain, or its flanking regions (Shatkina et al., 2003).
source: We have previously shown that the interaction of AR tau-5 is with the Bag-1L BAG domain, or its flanking regions (Shatkina et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shatkina et al., 2003.

claim: A triple mutation of K231/232/279A (CMut) was able to significantly decrease the interaction of AR and Bag-1L in a GST pull-down.
source: A triple mutation of K231/232/279A, referred to as CMut hereafter, was able to significantly decrease the interaction of AR and Bag-1L in a GST pull-down (Figure 2C) and co-IP experiment (Figure 2D), and reduce the AR NTD activity in a mammalian one-hybrid assay (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A triple mutation of K231/232/279A (CMut) was able to significantly decrease the interaction of AR and Bag-1L in a co-IP experiment.
source: A triple mutation of K231/232/279A, referred to as CMut hereafter, was able to significantly decrease the interaction of AR and Bag-1L in a GST pull-down (Figure 2C) and co-IP experiment (Figure 2D), and reduce the AR NTD activity in a mammalian one-hybrid assay (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: A triple mutation of K231/232/279A (CMut) was able to reduce the AR NTD activity in a mammalian one-hybrid assay.
source: A triple mutation of K231/232/279A, referred to as CMut hereafter, was able to significantly decrease the interaction of AR and Bag-1L in a GST pull-down (Figure 2C) and co-IP experiment (Figure 2D), and reduce the AR NTD activity in a mammalian one-hybrid assay (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Bag-1L CMut significantly altered the AR N/C-interaction compared to wild-type Bag-1L.
source: Additionally, Bag-1L CMut significantly altered the AR N/C-interaction compared to wild-type Bag-1L (Figure 2F), similar to what we observed in the FRET experiments in response to DHT treatment in the Bag-1L KO cells (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CMut Bag-1L- compared to wild-type Bag-1L-expressing cells displayed a reduction in AR chromatin binding by ChIP-seq.
source: CMut Bag-1L- compared to wild-type Bag-1L-expressing cells additionally displayed a reduction in AR chromatin binding by ChIP-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), similar to that described for the total loss of Bag-1L (Figure 1F), and a corresponding reduction in hormone-dependent AR function (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: CMut Bag-1L- compared to wild-type Bag-1L-expressing cells displayed a corresponding reduction in hormone-dependent AR function.
source: CMut Bag-1L- compared to wild-type Bag-1L-expressing cells additionally displayed a reduction in AR chromatin binding by ChIP-seq (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), similar to that described for the total loss of Bag-1L (Figure 1F), and a corresponding reduction in hormone-dependent AR function (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Several evolutionarily conserved residues within the BAG domain of Bag-1L (primarily in helices 2 and 3), when mutated, impair the ability of Bag-1L to enhance AR AF-1 transactivation to a similar extent as the CMut Bag-1L protein.
source: Moreover, we could show that several evolutionarily conserved residues within the BAG domain of Bag-1L (primarily in helices 2 and 3), when mutated, impair the ability of Bag-1L to enhance AR AF-1 transactivation to a similar extent as the CMut Bag-1L protein (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Mutating the BAG domain disrupts the Bag-1L:AR response similar to what we observed for the complete loss of Bag-1L.
source: This indicates that mutating the BAG domain disrupts the Bag-1L:AR response similar to what we observed for the complete loss of Bag-1L.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that BAG domain mutations have similar effects to Bag-1L loss.

claim: Association of AR, but not Hsp70 (HSPA1), was disrupted in Bag-1L biochemical complexes in the context of the triple mutation.
source: Association of AR, but not Hsp70 (HSPA1), was disrupted in Bag-1L biochemical complexes in the context of the triple mutation (Figure 2G); these data agree with the results of our GST pull-down (Figure 2C) and co-IP experiments (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Several proteins which exhibited decreased association with CMut Bag-1L are annotated with functional roles in protein synthesis, localization, or other aspects of proteostasis (Powers and Balch, 2013; Taipale et al., 2014; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015).
source: Several proteins which exhibited decreased association with CMut Bag-1L (Figure 2—source data 1) are annotated with functional roles in protein synthesis, localization, or other aspects of proteostasis (Powers and Balch, 2013; Taipale et al., 2014; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015) (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citations to Powers and Balch, 2013; Taipale et al., 2014; Labbadia and Morimoto, 2015.

claim: The dynamics observed in the biochemical complex as a function of the Bag1L mutant is consistent with the hypothesis that Bag-1L is involved in the folding of AR.
source: The dynamics we observed in the biochemical complex as a function of the Bag1L mutant is consistent with our hypothesis that Bag-1L is involved in the folding of AR (Figures 1G and 2F), suggesting a broader role for the BAG domain in proteome homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by data shown in Figures 1G and 2F.

claim: Bag-1L has a broader role for the BAG domain in proteome homeostasis.
source: The dynamics we observed in the biochemical complex as a function of the Bag1L mutant is consistent with our hypothesis that Bag-1L is involved in the folding of AR (Figures 1G and 2F), suggesting a broader role for the BAG domain in proteome homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is speculative, inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Comparison of the Cα and Cβ shifts revealed no significant changes in the wild-type and mutant BAG domain peptide, suggesting that the extent of α-helix formation is essentially unchanged for the two proteins.
source: Comparison of the Cα and Cβshifts revealed no significant changes in the wild-type and mutant BAG domain peptide (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), suggesting that the extent of α-helix formation is essentially unchanged for the two proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: About one third of residues that make the three antiparallel, helix bundles of the wild-type BAG domain (Briknarová et al., 2001) shifted to new positions or demonstrated reduced signal intensities in 1H15N-HSQC NMR spectra in response to the K231/232/279A mutations.
source: However, about one third of residues that make the three antiparallel, helix bundles of the wild-type BAG domain (Briknarová et al., 2001) shifted to new positions or demonstrated reduced signal intensities in 1H15N-HSQC NMR spectra in response to the K231/232/279A mutations (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6 and a citation to Briknarová et al., 2001.

claim: The three mutations cause a destabilization of the entire protein, a consequence of which is a significant change in the 3D-structure of Bag-1L and hence an altered interactome of CMut compared to wild-type Bag-1L.
source: This is most likely due to a destabilization of the entire protein caused by the three mutations, a consequence of which is a significant change in the 3D-structure of Bag-1L and hence an altered interactome of CMut compared to wild-type Bag-1L (Figure 2G).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Addition of the wild-type BAG peptide resulted in the reduction of resonance intensities within the C-terminal part of AR AF-1, indicating that these two molecules interact transiently.
source: Addition of the wild-type BAG peptide resulted in the reduction of resonance intensities within the C-terminal part of AR AF-1, indicating that these two molecules interact transiently (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The residues of AF-1 most affected by the interaction with the wild-type BAG domain corresponded to tau-5 and were previously identified as partially folded by NMR (De Mol et al., 2016).
source: The residues of AF-1 most affected by this interaction corresponded to tau-5 and were previously identified as partially folded by NMR (De Mol et al., 2016), suggesting that the wild-type BAG domain interacts preferentially with this sub-domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to De Mol et al., 2016.

claim: The wild-type BAG domain interacts preferentially with the tau-5 sub-domain.
source: The residues of AF-1 most affected by this interaction corresponded to tau-5 and were previously identified as partially folded by NMR (De Mol et al., 2016), suggesting that the wild-type BAG domain interacts preferentially with this sub-domain.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Moderate decreases in intensity were also observed in tau-1, in the region centered around residue 275, which has the propensity to adopt extended conformations.
source: Moderate decreases in intensity were also observed in tau-1, in the region centered around residue 275, which has the propensity to adopt extended conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Although Bag-1L through its BAG domain binds tau-5, the interaction propagates to tau-1.
source: This suggests that although Bag-1L through its BAG domain binds tau-5, the interaction propagates to tau-1.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: Equivalent experiments carried out with the BAG domain mutant showed a much-attenuated effect, indicating that the strength of the interaction was diminished by the mutations.
source: Equivalent experiments carried out with the BAG domain mutant showed a much-attenuated effect, indicating that the strength of the interaction was diminished by the mutations, which agrees with our previous results (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Although all 44 structures lack a classical 'druggable' site (defined as sites that harbor geometric and physiochemical properties consistent with binding orally-bioavailable small molecules with strict drug-like properties) (Tym et al., 2016), a large 'ligandable' cavity was identified, which is druggable using peptides or peptidomimetic drugs.
source: Although all 44 structures lack a classical 'druggable' site (defined as sites that harbor geometric and physiochemical properties consistent with binding orally-bioavailable small molecules with strict drug-like properties) (Tym et al., 2016), we were able to identify a large 'ligandable' cavity, which is druggable using peptides or peptidomimetic drugs (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis and a citation to Tym et al., 2016.

claim: The three amino acids (K231/232/279) important for AR binding lie within (K231 and 232) or just outside the edge (K279) of the ligandable cavity.
source: Moreover, we could demonstrate that the three amino acids (K231/232/279) important for AR binding lie within (K231 and 232) or just outside the edge (K279) of this cavity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Mutation of residues K231 and K232 jointly, but not K279 alone, reduced the binding to AR.
source: This agrees with our independent findings from the pull-down and luciferase assay (Figure 2C and E), where mutation of residues K231 and K232 jointly, but not K279 alone, reduced the binding to AR.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and E.

claim: In these experiments the biggest effect was achieved in response to a simultaneous mutation of all three residues, suggesting that the triple mutant behaves similarly to the complete loss of Bag-1L.
source: However, in these experiments the biggest effect was achieved in response to a simultaneous mutation of all three residues, suggesting that the triple mutant behaves similarly to the complete loss of Bag-1L.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental results.

claim: The overlap between these experimental results and the computational prediction of the cavity suggests that pharmacological interference with the predicted cavity of Bag-1L is highly likely to impair AR action.
source: The overlap between these experimental results and the computational prediction of the cavity suggests that pharmacological interference with the predicted cavity of Bag-1L is highly likely to impair AR action.
evidence: This claim is speculative, based on the combination of experimental and computational results.

claim: Thio-2 has previously been postulated to bind to the BAG domain and to inhibit the interaction between Hsp70 and Bag-1 (Enthammer et al., 2013; Papadakis et al., 2016).
source: Thio-2 has previously been postulated to bind to the BAG domain and to inhibit the interaction between Hsp70 and Bag-1 (Enthammer et al., 2013; Papadakis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Enthammer et al., 2013 and Papadakis et al., 2016.

claim: Overexpression of Bag-1 is commonly observed in drug-resistant cell lines (Ding et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2009).
source: This is in line with previous reports that overexpression of nuclear Bag-1 correlates with drug resistance (Ni et al., 2013) and that Bag-1 overexpression is commonly observed in drug-resistant cell lines (Ding et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ding et al., 2000; Chen et al., 2002; Liu et al., 2009.

claim: Thio-2 was able to abrogate the endogenous Bag-1L:AR interaction in LNCaP cells.
source: Thio-2 was indeed able to abrogate the endogenous Bag-1L:AR interaction in LNCaP cells (Figure 4A), as well as inhibit the androgen-dependent LNCaP cell growth (IC50 = 17.5 μM; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Thio-2 was able to inhibit the androgen-dependent LNCaP cell growth (IC50 = 17.5 μM).
source: Thio-2 was indeed able to abrogate the endogenous Bag-1L:AR interaction in LNCaP cells (Figure 4A), as well as inhibit the androgen-dependent LNCaP cell growth (IC50 = 17.5 μM; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Thio-2, unlike the AR N-terminal inhibitors EPI-001 or ido-EPI-002 (Andersen et al., 2010) and the AR LBD inhibitor enzalutamide, was able to effectively suppress Bag-1L function in a mammalian-1H assay.

claim: Targeting Bag-1L through inhibition of its BAG domain, is a therapeutic possibility to abrogate AR function and reduce PCa growth.

claim: Re-expression of wild-type Bag-1L was able to rescue the growth inhibition triggered by Bag-1L KO.

claim: Re-expression of the vector or Bag-1L CMut failed to rescue the growth inhibition triggered by Bag-1L KO.

claim: Wild-type Bag-1L overexpression promotes growth in mouse xenograft experiments, in intact animals.

claim: Overexpression of wild-type Bag-1L did not cause an increase in CRPC growth in LNCaP-abl and LNCaP95 cells.

claim: There was little change in cytoplasmic Bag-1 expression (p=0.14) in the progression from HSPC to CRPC.
